{{short description|Japanese mathematician}}
{{family name hatnote|Kurushima|lang=Japanese}}

{{nihongo|'''Kurushima Kinai'''|久留島 喜内||died January 9, 1757}},<ref>[http://www.math.s.chiba-u.ac.jp/~kitazume/kinai.html 久留島喜内]  -- [[Chiba University]], [http://www.math.s.chiba-u.ac.jp/ Dept. of Mathematics and Informatics]</ref> also known as 
'''Kurushima Yoshita'''<ref name="clark">[http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/mathhist/japan.html  List of Japanese mathematicians] -- [[Clark University]], <!-- David E. Joyce --> [http://aleph0.clarku.edu/~djoyce/mathhist/mathhist.html   Dept. of Mathematics and Computer Science]</ref> and {{nihongo|'''Kurushima Yoshihiro'''|久留島 義太}},<ref name="yoshihiro">[http://www.oclc.org/research/activities/identities/default.htm  WorldCat Identities] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101230150412/http://www.oclc.org/research/activities/identities/default.htm |date=2010-12-30 }}: [http://www.worldcat.org/identities/np-kurushima,%20yoshihiro$1757   久留島義太 -1757]</ref> was a Japanese [[mathematician]] in the [[Edo period]].<ref>Smith, David. (1914). {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|''A History of Japanese Mathematics,'' p. 176. |page=176}}</ref>

The Japanese board game of [[shogi]] attracted Kurushima's interest; and he was recognized in his own time as a master player.<ref>[[Shogi]], [https://www.youtube.com/view_play_list?p=DEC088C073AFC7BE "Famous Mate Problems" -- #62, #63, #68, #69, #79]</ref>  Among shogi players, he continues today to be well known for seven "puzzle ring" [[gambit]]s with subsequent sequenced maneuvers—including the "silver puzzle ring."<ref>''La Revue de l'Association Française de Shogi,'' Juillet 1998, Numéro 19, p. 4.</ref>

In his lifetime, he was recognized among the most prominent intellectuals. His mathematical gift was highly esteemed.<ref>Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|p. 166. |page=166}}</ref>  Kurushima, like most of his contemporaries, was very interested in the mathematical problems involved in "magic squares."<ref name="jochi38">Michiwaka, Yoshimasa. (1997). "Magic Squares in Japanese Mathematics," {{Google books|raKRY3KQspsC&dq| ''Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures,'' p. 539. |page=539}}</ref>
